title: Benchmarking Open-Source O-RAN and 5G NTN Stacks on Embedded ARM Platforms for Space Payloads
summary: Regenerative satellite payloads, which host the 5G Next Generation Node B (gNB) onboard instead of transparently relaying the radio signal, are a key building block of the Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) integration that 3GPP started in Release 17. Combining them with the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture adds software-defined control through RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs), enabling in-orbit reconfiguration, multi-tenancy, and data-driven radio resource management. Open-source implementations make this vision accessible to research institutions and New Space missions, yet there is little quantitative evidence on how they behave on the embedded processors that a satellite can actually carry. This paper presents an out-of-the-box experimental benchmark of two open-source gNB stacks (i.e., OpenAirInterface/Duranta and srsRAN/OCUDU), and two Near-Real-Time RICs (i.e., the ORAN-SC Near-RT RIC and FlexRIC). All components are deployed on an ARMv8 platform representative of the processing units used in small-satellite payloads, driving a USRP B210 software-defined radio. We compare them in terms of functional compliance (3GPP NTN features, O-RAN interfaces, multi-tenancy), resource efficiency, real-time behavior, and engineering suitability. Results show that these platforms can host a joint gNB + near-RT RIC deployment using any of the considered components, although further optimizations are still required for carrier-grade performance. However, the performance and standards compliance vary significantly among them. Building on these results, we derive a decision framework that maps mission profiles and Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) budgets to gNB/near-RT RIC combinations. Finally, we discuss the open gaps remaining before these stacks can be flown in NTN regenerative payloads.

title: SimPyWireless: A PHY-Aware Discrete-Event Simulation Framework for Wi-Fi and 5G NR-U Coexistence in the 5 GHz Band
summary: The growing demand from heterogeneous wireless applications with stringent QoS and QoE requirements is increasing pressure on available spectrum resources. Although mmWave and THz bands offer additional capacity, their propagation and hardware limitations make sub-6~GHz unlicensed spectrum, particularly the 5~GHz band, an attractive complementary resource. However, reproducible Wi-Fi/5G NR-U coexistence studies remain limited by the lack of lightweight, open-source, PHY-aware simulation platforms. We present SimPyWireless, a discrete-event simulation framework for Wi-Fi and 5G NR-U coexistence in the 5~GHz unlicensed band. The framework integrates shared-channel modeling, propagation, interference, SINR, heterogeneous traffic, mobility, and technology-specific channel access, while providing modular support for externally trained AI/ML models. We validate SimPyWireless against an analytical DTMC model and demonstrate expected coexistence behavior under varying contention and mobility conditions. SimPyWireless provides a reproducible and extensible middle ground between analytical modeling and hardware-based experimentation.

title: Intent-Defined Radio: A Goal-Native Architecture for Next-Generation Wireless Networks
summary: Wireless systems are becoming harder to operate because service goals are increasingly expressed in outcome-oriented terms, while radio platforms still expose mainly low-level configurations and protocol-specific controls. This mismatch makes it difficult to translate latency, reliability, throughput, and continuity requirements into coherent radio behavior. This article argues for Intent-Defined Radio (IDR) as a new system abstraction for next-generation wireless networks. Rather than treating the radio stack as a fixed mechanism set to be manually engineered and then tuned, IDR connects explicit service goals to executable radio behavior within a constrained design space by leveraging the capacity of large language models (LLMs). We position IDR relative to programmable radio, intent-based networking, and learning-based protocol design. We also present two simulation studies using Intent2MAC to illustrate the design loop, demonstrating executable MAC synthesis and offline refinement guided by evaluation feedback. The results show improved service satisfaction at a throughput cost and improved remote-control performance when random contention is replaced by distributed urgency-based arbitration. We finally discuss the open challenges in intent specification, evidence, hardware execution, interoperability, and lifecycle cost, and outline a staged path toward deployment.

title: An LLM-Driven Traffic-Control xApp for Dynamic 5G RAN Intents
summary: Programmable Radio Access Networks (RANs) enable runtime deployment of traffic-control functions, but selecting the appropriate configuration remains challenging as network conditions and service requirements change over time. Conventional solutions often rely on static rules or learning-based controllers with predefined state and action spaces, limiting their ability to accommodate changing intents. This paper introduces an LLM-driven xApp for traffic control in programmable RANs. The proposed architecture combines operator-defined service intents, runtime E2 interface telemetry, and the currently deployed configuration to generate traffic-management policies without blocking packet forwarding or the processing of incoming E2 measurements during LLM inference. Experiments on an OpenAirInterface 5G environment show that the proposed controller dynamically adapts the traffic-control pipeline to runtime intent changes, achieving an average intent satisfaction ratio of 0.91, compared with 0.52 for a static TC-RAN configuration. When channel conditions degrade, the controller maintains an intent satisfaction ratio of approx. 0.88, compared with approx. 0.4 for the static baseline.

title: Adaptive Filtering With Reduced Computational Complexity Using SOPOT Arithmetic
summary: Implementing finite impulse response (FIR) adaptive filters by employing the sums of signed-powers-of-two (SOPOT) arithmetic may lead to simpler hardware and consequently reduced power consumption. In this paper, one evaluates the effects of SOPOT arithmetic on the adaptive filter's recursion algorithms. The filters' coefficients and algorithms' underlying variables are fully operated using SOPOT arithmetic in the whole iterative process. More specifically, one evaluates convergence rate, numerical stability, and accuracy since using few signed-powers-of-two (SPT) terms propagates numerical errors during the adaptive cycle that may impair the algorithm behavior. The SOPOT approximations are obtained through the technique known as Matching Pursuits with Generalized Bit-Plane (MPGBP) algorithm, with notable cost-performance trade-off and low computational complexity. Results are provided for the Least-Mean-Squares (LMS), the Normalized Least-Mean-Squares (NLMS) and the Recursive-Least-Squares (RLS) algorithms, considering adaptive filters employed for system identification and change detection.

title: There is no binary linear $[65,9,29]$ code
summary: We prove that no binary linear $[65,9,\geqslant29]$ code exists, equivalently, that no even binary linear $[66,9,\geqslant30]$ code exists. Together with known constructions, this determines $d_2(65,9)=28$, $n_2(9,29)=66$, and $n_2(9,30)=67$. A residual-code bound and a known construction also give $d_2(122,10)=56$. To prove nonexistence, we associate with a hypothetical even code a quadratic function derived from half the codeword weight modulo $2$. Its polar form determines the fourth derivative of a Boolean function of degree at most four. Character sums, weight moments, and the exclusion of weight-$42$ codewords give upper bounds on the support of this function in seven cases. Restrictions to nondegenerate affine subspaces exclude six cases. In the remaining case, equality would force four distinct coordinate functionals to be identically $1$ on an affine seven-space, although at most two can have this property. The argument uses published minimum-length results for binary linear codes of dimensions eight and nine.

title: Asymmetric Transistor Aging Under Thermal Gradients
summary: Advanced technology nodes improve performance but increase susceptibility to BTI-induced aging. Using aging- aware circuit simulations, we show that realistic on-chip thermal gradients can cause significant asymmetric transistor degradation in 16 nm FinFET circuits, leading to setup and hold time violations. These results highlight the necessity of incorporating thermal-gradient-aware aging analysis into timing signoff to ensure chip reliability.

title: Ties at the Top: A Point-in-Time Comparison of CVSS and EPSS at a Fixed Budget
summary: Organizations must decide which vulnerabilities warrant further analysis and protective action when the volume of published vulnerabilities exceeds their analytical capacity. We present a methodology for comparing vulnerability-prioritization strategies under an explicit resource constraint, represented by a fixed number of CVEs selected from a common eligible population. We apply this methodology to the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS). For CVEs published in the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) from 17 March to 31 December 2025 and from 1 January to 31 March 2026 (Q1), we reconstruct each CVE's scores and status 30 days after NVD publication, using archived source data. Each cohort has one ranking per strategy at a 5% budget. Positives are CVEs added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog within 180 days after their decision day. The catalog is maintained by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). EPSS captures 16 of 40 positives in 2025, versus 5 for CVSS; alternative selections among tied CVEs cannot raise CVSS capture above 9. In Q1, CVSS captures 4 of 11 and EPSS 3, but tie-breaking can reverse this ordering. The score alone leaves most of each CVSS list undecided: the tie-breaking rule allocates 1,678 of 1,919 CVSS places in 2025 and 589 of 758 in Q1 among CVEs tied at score 9.8. Most chosen CVSS scores come from non-NVD providers; disabling those scores reduces CVSS capture from 5 to 1 in 2025 and from 4 to 0 in Q1. A fixed-budget comparison should therefore report its decision cutoff, eligible population, score provenance, and tie-breaking rule.

title: PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction
comment: Accepted to the KDD 2027 AI for Sciences Track
summary: Understanding how stable psychometric traits and time-varying states jointly inform behavior is an important problem in computational behavioral science. Existing personalized agents commonly condition actions directly on a static profile, leaving realized state transitions unused as an explicit source of supervision. We introduce a profile-conditioned state world model that uses observed environment--behavior state transitions to learn transition-informed representations for behavioral prediction. During training, a posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions, while a prior predicts the resulting codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context. The prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator-grounded execution. Thus, the world model provides structured transition supervision instead of treating personality as a direct action descriptor. We evaluate the framework in VEET, a controlled behavioral simulator with human trajectories, and in AgentSociety as a structurally different synthetic environment. A participant-disjoint split of 240 training, 25 validation, and 48 test participants evaluates generalization to unseen people. On VEET, the model reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95\% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL. Ablations associate continuous next-state modeling with most of the Top-1 gain, while discrete codes and prior alignment mainly improve Top-3 and distributional alignment. These results establish transition-informed world-model supervision as useful for subject-generalized behavior prediction, without implying causal psychological mechanisms or calibrated long-horizon state dynamics.

title: Software-Defined Internet Integration of Satellite Networks (SDISN)
summary:
This paper proposes SDISN, a software-defined Internet integration of satellite networks. It facilitates the transmission of IP traffic from user terminals (UTs) or Internet nodes over a satellite network with inter-satellite links (ISLs). Gateways (GWs) together with Points of Presence (PoPs) support the transition between the satellite network and the Internet. UTs and GWs connect to the satellite network via serving satellites (SrvSats). As the satellites orbit the Earth at high speed, UTs and GWs frequently change their SrvSats. This causes frequent changes to their reachability, which poses a major challenge for integration.
  In the proposed solution, GWs and SrvSats encapsulate traffic with forwarding information so that the traffic can be carried over the satellite network towards appropriate SrvSats of UTs or GWs. The forwarding information on the encapsulating nodes is continuously updated by a controller to reflect changed SrvSats and possibly changed topology of the satellite network. Design goals for the proposed architecture were low complexity on satellites, high ability for traffic engineering, and keeping UTs out of the routing system for security and compatibility reasons.
  UTs may have increased security requirements (ISRs) such that their traffic should be carried within the constellation to avoid non-trusted terrestrial infrastructure. Extensions are proposed to support such ISRs. UTs may obtain either dynamic IP addresses from a nearby GW/PoP wherever they roam or they may obtain static IP addresses from a fixed Home GW/PoP. In the latter case, triangle routing via the Home GW occurs when the UT roams away from the Home GW. As this adds latency to the communication, we investigate architectural extensions for latency reduction. In addition, we show how traffic engineering can be performed in such an architecture with the help of alternate GWs and SrvSats.

title: AE-DISC: Automorphism Ensemble Direct-Invocation Successive Cancellation for Low-Latency Decoding
summary: Emerging applications in hyper-reliable low-latency communication (HRLLC) demand channel decoders that deliver deterministic performance under stringent latency and reliability constraints. While Polar codes are well suited for this scenario due to their strong error-correction capability, conventional successive cancellation (SC) decoding exhibits inherent serial dependencies that lead to high decoding latency. This paper presents the automorphism ensemble direct-invocation successive cancellation (AE-DISC) decoder, a low-latency framework that enables the concurrent computation of the left and right decoding subtrees in the SC process, yielding substantial speed-ups. By exploiting permutation automorphisms, AE-DISC decoding further improves error-correction performance. Simulation results demonstrate that AE-DISC attains up to 1.4 dB gain over the 5G SC baseline and surpasses layered min-sum (LMS) low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoders at a frame error rate (FER) of $10^{-6}$, while maintaining fixed algorithmic complexity. Both theoretical analysis and application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) synthesis results further show up to 2 times decoding speed-up relative to fast simplified successive cancellation (FSSC).

title: Structure and Complexity of Perfect Functional Representations
comment: 19 pages, 1 figure. Extended version of "On Perfect Functional Representations", presented at the 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT) with complete proofs and additional results
summary: For given random variables $(X,Y)$, functional representation lemma states that there exists a random variable $Z$ and a deterministic function $g$ such that $Y = g(X,Z)$, and $X$ is independent of $Z$. In other words, $Z$ captures all the information about $Y$ not contained in $X$. We refer to $Z$ as a `perfect functional representation' if it satisfies $I(Y;Z) = H(Y|X)$. We show that the existence of perfect representation depends solely on the conditional distribution $p_{Y|X}$ and define the corresponding conditional distributions as perfectly representable. We provide a necessary and sufficient condition for $p_{Y|X}$ to be perfectly representable. Moreover, we cast the problem of checking perfect representability as a linear program, give an algorithm whose complexity is polynomial in $|\mathcal Y|$ and exponential in $|\mathcal X|$, and prove that deciding perfect representability is NP-complete for rational input matrices encoded in binary.

title: An α-potential linear approximation for LQ differential games
summary: Feedback Nash equilibria of infinite-horizon linear-quadratic (LQ) differential games are characterized by coupled algebraic Riccati equations (cAREs), whose numerical solution generally relies on iterative algorithms and can be highly sensitive to their initialization. Motivated by the $α$-potential-game framework, this letter proposes an $α$-potential linear approximation for constructing a systematic, game-dependent initialization. For an N-player LQ game, a reference potential game is constructed. Its equilibrium requires solving only one standard algebraic Riccati equation. The original cAREs are subsequently linearized around this reference solution, yielding a coupled linear system whose solution provides player-specific corrections and hence an approximate feedback Nash equilibrium. The resulting approximation is used to initialize three standard cARE solvers. Numerical experiments on $10^4$ randomly generated two-player games show that the proposed initialization reduces the mean number of iterations. Further experiments for $N=2,\ldots,13$ show that the reduction in iteration count persists as the number of players increases.

title: Signed, Valid, and Unauthorized: Authority Closure at the Trust Boundary Between Agent Commerce Protocols and Crypto Wallets
summary: Agent commerce protocols let software agents pay with stablecoins. A buyer approves a payee, asset, spending cap and time window, but the wallet signs an object whose effects depend on the contracts that consume it. Matching the displayed fields or simulating one payment can miss transfers that the signed object still permits. We define authority closure as the set of transfer sequences that holding the signed object can enable. A wallet object respects the mandate when every such sequence meets the buyer's constraints. We characterize when wallet objects can satisfy this property and implement Closure, a wallet-side checker covering 13 families of signed objects. In an evaluation of 2,130 generated objects and 62,979 execution programs, 265 objects with an observed violation passed both a field-and-expiry check and an address allow-list. Under the test model, Closure rejected all 1,680 objects with an observed violation and accepted the remaining 450. In two local checkouts using the x402 reference client, approved payments settled and Closure refused requests outside the mandate before signing. The median decision time was at most 12 microseconds per family.

title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
summary:
Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model.
  At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps.
  Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.

title: A Brief Overview of Non-Terrestrial Networks (Updated 2026)
summary: This article extends the 2023 preprint \emph{A brief introduction to satellite communications for Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN)} (\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04590v1}{arXiv:2305.04590v1}) with a revision of its foundations, tables and state of the art as of 18 November 2026. It revisits propagation, link budgets, spectrum reuse and phased arrays, including corrected equations and numerical examples. Updated tables distinguish operational, launched and planned constellations and compare published fixed-terminal rates with direct-to-device services. The discussion incorporates developments in 3GPP Releases 17--20, commercial LTE-based direct-to-cell services and research towards 6G non-terrestrial networks. Operator announcements are distinguished from independent measurements and future plans. Open challenges include spectrum coordination, Doppler and timing compensation, mobility, capacity, security and the sustainability of low Earth orbit.

title: Conditional-Hierarchical Open-Set Deep Learning for Robust Radio Signals Intelligence
summary: This paper proposes an open-set radio-frequency (RF) deep learning (DL) framework that jointly performs conditionally hierarchical multi-level radio signal classification and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. To exploit image-based classification models, the raw radio samples are transformed into time-frequency representations using the short time Fourier transform (STFT) to pre-process the radio signals. A lightweight novel architecture using neural network (CNN), that applies con- ditional hierarchical multi-task classification heads, is introduced, and compared to two baselines including: (1) The conventional convolutional neural network (CNN) and (2) Swin-T model with multitask classification heads, where the model accuracy and complexity perspectives are considered for the comparison. Moreover, to address open-set scenarios, we introduce the fusion of two OOD detectors each of which is fitted to a Gaussian mixture model by using the learned feature space (e.g. the feature embeddings and logits) from the multi-head classifica- tion network. The overall training process is achieved on two stages following a post-hoc design: the in-set classification neural network is trained first, then the learnable parameters are frozen in the evaluation mode to process the training dataset again to aggregate the embeddings and logits used to fit the GMMs for OOD detection. Moreover, a proof of concept using experimental setup is implemented to validate the operation of the introduced models and algorithms in practical scenarios. The simulation- based trained model is fine-tuned using experimentally measured radio signals. For the experimental setup, a USRP-B210 acting as a transmitter, and an edge Deepwave Air-T software-defined radio, which is equipped with the fine-tuned neural networks is used as a detector or receiver.

title: Generalized Covering radii and Deep Holes of a Family of Antiprimitive Narrow-Sense BCH Codes in Even Characteristic
summary: This paper determines the generalized covering radii, deep holes, and complete coset leader weight distribution of the antiprimitive narrow-sense BCH code of length \(q+1\) and designed distance \(3\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), where \(q=2^m\) and \(m\geq 2\). We establish the complete generalized covering-radius hierarchy: the covering radius is \(3\), whereas the \(t\)-th generalized covering radius is \(4\) for every \(t\geq 2\). Using the covering radius, we then derive necessary and sufficient conditions for a received word to be a deep hole by reducing the syndrome representations to conditions involving roots of an associated cubic polynomial. An explicit parametrization yields complete, nonredundant representatives of all deep-hole cosets. Enumerating these representatives gives closed-form expressions for the numbers of deep holes and determines the complete coset leader weight distribution, with distinct formulas according to the parity of \(m\).

title: Reliability-based Sizing of Energy Storage for Large Load Integration
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, published as part of the proceedings of the 2026 Grid of the Future Symposium organized by the CIGRE US National Committee
summary: The number of large loads connected to the bulk power system has been increasing rapidly worldwide. Emerging high-demand facilities, particularly AI data centers, are introducing new challenges for power system planners. In absence of appropriate planning mechanisms, the addition of high volumes of data center loads will lead to an increase in outages, thus degrading reliability of the system. Energy storage systems (ESS) offer a promising solution to mitigate the reliability impacts of these large loads, due to their flexibility and fast-ramping characteristics. However, ESS should be judiciously sized and sited to maximize the reliability benefits to the grid. This paper presents a framework for the optimal sizing and siting of ESS to minimize the adverse reliability impacts of large load additions. First, a stochastic semi-Markov model is developed to model the load of AI data centers and generate profiles for several such facilities. These profiles are then incorporated into a Markov-chain Monte Carlo simulation-based composite system reliability assessment framework. A detailed nodal network model is used to quantify the reliability impacts of adding data centers and to identify buses most affected by large loads. Resource adequacy metrics are used to evaluate the overall system reliability impacts. ESS are then strategically sized and sited based on this analysis to mitigate the negative impacts of large loads on overall system reliability. The proposed framework is demonstrated using the RTS-GMLC 72-bus test system. The results show how ESS can effectively enhance system reliability in the presence of rapidly growing large-load demand. This framework provides system planners, utilities, and regulators with a practical tool for maintaining reliable power system operation using energy storage as more large loads are integrated into the grid.

title: Attacks and Defenses in Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Hop-by-Hop Task Decomposition and Delegation
summary:
Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems enable independently administered agents, each with its own operator, model, memory, and configuration, to collaborate on complex tasks without centralized coordination. Agents autonomously decompose tasks, execute subtasks and delegate remaining work to peers, enabling scalability and eliminating single points of failure. However, decentralization also introduces significant security challenges, as no single entity has complete visibility into task execution or the authority to enforce correct behavior across agents.
  In this paper, we systematize threats from malicious agents in decentralized multi-agent systems and propose mitigation techniques. We first design and evaluate attacks against integrity, availability, and confidentiality, demonstrating that a single malicious agent can cause up to 100% task failure, inflate token consumption and runtime by up to 7.7x and 3.2x, respectively, and exfiltrate up to 94% of relevant prior tasks from benign agents. We then present a cryptographic protocol that produces an irrefutable verified execution trace of every action taken in the system and develop an auditor that analyzes these traces to detect and attribute malicious behavior. Evaluations on HiddenBench using gpt-6.1-sol and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 show that our protocol incurs negligible latency overhead, while the auditor detects and correctly attributes 98% of attacks, including those that comply with the protocol.

title: Density Feedback Control for Transferability of Generative Sparse Adversarial Attacks
summary: Generator-based sparse adversarial attacks train encoder--decoder networks to produce transferable sparse perturbations for black-box robustness evaluation. Their perturbation density, however, is set only indirectly by a fixed sparsity coefficient whose mapping to density is unknown and shifts during training, so reaching a target density requires re-tuning; this fixed pressure also yields little transferability gain once density reduction begins. We propose Density Feedback Control (DFC), which tightens or relaxes this coefficient at the end of each epoch according to the gap between the observed hard-mask density and the target, without changing the generator architecture or loss. At a 10\% target density, DFC brings the mean density of three base attacks within one percentage point of the target in a single run and improves the transfer attack success rate (ASR) of two of them on CNN and Transformer targets, including under per-image $\ell_0$ budgets, while perturbing fewer pixels. Tracing GPG's training, we observe that as DFC relaxes the coefficient, the transfer ASR recovers with the density and overtakes the fixed-coefficient baseline with fewer pixels. For EGS-TSSA, which restricts perturbations to source-model feature-importance regions, DFC yields no consistent gain; we analyze how this restriction interacts with density feedback.

title: ScaleWire: An End-to-End Scale-Up Ethernet Simulation Framework for LLM Systems
summary: LLM training and inference rely on scale-up networks for high-bandwidth, low-latency memory-semantic communication among accelerators (XPUs). Ethernet is emerging as an open interconnect for scale-up systems. In Ethernet systems, network-interface (NI) mechanisms across transport, network, and link layers interact, jointly shaping communication performance and on-chip resource requirements. We present ScaleWire, an end-to-end scale-up Ethernet simulation framework for LLM systems. It couples packet-level simulation of cross-layer NI mechanisms with a resource exploration engine that combines analytical estimates and simulation to size on-chip resources. We validate ScaleWire against hardware measurements and nine analytical checks, and evaluate six NI designs across four LLM communication workloads. For DeepSeek-R1 dispatch, NI design choices lead to a 4.5$\times$ difference in per-XPU on-chip storage budget. In grid-comparison experiments, the exploration engine uses 6-19% of the simulations required by exhaustive search. Using vLLM prefill traces with kernel times measured on GH200 GPUs, ScaleWire further guides resource provisioning under a completion-time constraint for inference execution. ScaleWire thus helps designers select NI mechanisms and provision on-chip resources to balance communication performance and resource cost.

title: Distributed Fiber Monitoring on a Coherent DSP ASIC: Implementation of Longitudinal Power Monitoring
summary: Coherent DSP ASICs and transceivers to date report a rich set of optical link metrics, yet these remain cumulative over the link and provide no spatial localization. This paper presents the implementation design of fiber-longitudinal power monitoring (LPM), which recovers spatially resolved power profiles from received traffic, on a coherent DSP ASIC chip. We first identify the challenges specific to DSP implementation, and describe the enabling algorithm and architecture. We then present the key design considerations for retaining the estimation fidelity of the on-chip LPM during in-service operation. On this basis, we implement LPM on a coherent DSP, a 3-nm 800G low-power DSP ASIC housed in an OSFP pluggable module, which constitutes, to our knowledge, the first coherent DSP ASIC and transceiver to perform distributed fiber monitoring and data communication simultaneously. The on-chip LPM is experimentally validated over links of up to 1005 km using 400ZR+ and 800ZR+ traffic, with no measurable impact on Q factor or module power consumption. Multi-vendor interoperability is also demonstrated, where the on-chip LPM operates on signals transmitted by third-party transceivers. These results extend coherent DSPs from cumulative to spatially resolved monitoring, allowing pluggable transceivers, deployable from DCI to long-haul, to act not only as cost-efficient transmission elements but also as distributed monitoring points across diverse optical network infrastructure.

title: Improved Constants in the Kautz-Singleton Construction for Probabilistic Group Testing
summary: We consider the probabilistic nonadaptive group testing problem, in which a uniformly random defective set of size $d$ is to be identified among $N$ items using a binary test matrix. For the explicit Kautz--Singleton construction, it is known that order-optimal scaling $T=Θ(d\log N)$ for high-probability recovery can be achieved in the regime $d=Ω(\log^2 N)$. However, the leading constant in this scaling remains uncharacterized even for standard low-complexity decoders. In this work, we revisit the probabilistic analysis of this construction and improve the leading constant for the COMP decoder, as well as establishing the same bound for the DD decoder. Our approach relies on a sharper analysis of the number of distinct roots associated with the defective items, yielding tighter bounds on the decoding error probability. In particular, we show that both COMP and DD achieve vanishing average error probability with $T\le (1/\ln 2+\varepsilon)d\log N$ tests for any $\varepsilon>0$, in the admissible regime $N=q^k$ for some prime power $q = Θ(d)$ and integer $k \ge 2$. For COMP, this leading constant matches that of the random near-constant column weight design, whereas for DD, a gap remains except in the sparse regime $d = N^{o(1)}$.

title: Stochastic Crew Placement for Winter Storm Restoration of Rural Distribution Feeders Considering Building Cooling Deadlines
summary: Winter storm outages on rural distribution feeders may leave electrically heated houses cooling below acceptable indoor temperatures. This paper proposes a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer linear program for pre-storm crew placement that considers the building cooling deadline. Crews are placed before the storm, and repairs and reconnection are scheduled in each damage scenario to minimize the expected cost. Specifically, outage house-hours beyond the deadline are penalized, and feeder voltage and loading constraints account for cold load pickup at each reconnection. A case study on a synthetic rural feeder shows that the penalty shifts one of two crews toward a remote village, reducing expected house-hours beyond the deadline by 39 percent for 5.3 percent more outage house-hours. With three crews, the penalty does not change crew placement. Immediate reconnection would violate the voltage limit in four of six scenarios.

title: PriTabICL: Differentially Private Tabular In-Context Learning with Task-Aligned Cluster-Wise Synthesis
summary:
Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict target records using a handful of labeled demonstrations in their prompts. However, these demonstrations often contain sensitive personal information. Differential privacy (DP) offers principled protection, but noise-based methods introduce substantial noise, distorting the feature-label relationships essential for accurate prediction, especially as data dimensionality grows.
  In this work, we study DP data synthesis for generating privacy-preserving TabICL demonstrations. We identify two limitations of directly applying general-purpose DP synthesis to entire datasets: modeling a global distribution can obscure local structure and minority patterns in heterogeneous data, while measuring broad attribute dependencies under a limited privacy budget can reduce the accuracy available for relationships most relevant to prediction. More broadly, global statistical fidelity may fail to preserve heterogeneous structures needed by downstream predictive and generative models. To address these challenges, we propose PriTabICL, a general framework compatible with existing DP synthesis algorithms. It partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each independently, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistical relationships. At inference, each query is routed to a DP cluster, and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic dataset without additional privacy loss for the original records. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across heterogeneous datasets. In particular, one of our instantiations, PriTabICL-PrivSyn, improves over global PrivSyn in 8 out of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings. Open-source code is available.

title: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
summary: Language models often produce high-quality individual samples but poor sets, with repeated samples clustering around the same semantic modes. We formalize diverse generation as sampling a size-$K$ subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where the likelihood encodes item quality, and the embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Exact inference over all strings is intractable, so we propose PoolDPP: draw a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weight the candidates toward the target quality, and run a $K$-DPP sampler on the induced pool kernel; a greedy MAP variant provides deterministic selection. We prove a finite-sample bound with an explicit constant: the KL divergence between the sampler's output and the target $K$-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size. Empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality--diversity frontier on open-ended generation and the precision--recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (Ambrosia), and on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), it raises diversity at about the same pass@$K$.

title: RouterWeave: A Unified Observation Layer for Cross-Platform Activity Analysis via Home Routers
summary: Smart homes bring together devices from different operating systems and vendor ecosystems, but each platform reports activity only for the devices and features it supports, leaving gaps in household-wide activity monitoring. Interoperability standards such as Matter and software integrations connect and control supported devices, yet vendor restrictions and licensing barriers limit access to their data, while hardware constraints hinder integration. Our key insight is that encrypted network traffic provides complementary evidence of activity across platform boundaries. Accordingly, we present RouterWeave, a router-side observation framework that combines cross-platform traffic collection, task-adaptive processing, and unified activity records. These records preserve activity meaning, temporal extent, and source-device attribution while distinguishing discrete operations from sustained activity intervals. We evaluate RouterWeave across four datasets, native execution on a commodity home router, and two novel case studies: cross-platform Screen Time monitoring and appliance energy estimation. RouterWeave achieves 94.41% macro-F1 on application activities and 97.46% on IoT operations, outperforming baselines by up to 20.99 percentage points, while using under 7 MB of router memory per task and supporting 54 concurrent devices within a 5-second update window. In end-to-end case studies, RouterWeave reconstructs 600 Screen Time timelines across Android, iOS, and Windows with 92.15% accuracy (24.84-second mean active-time error over 19-minute averages) and recovers 49 of 55 appliance operations over four days, tracking ON/OFF states with 92.84% agreement and estimating electricity use within a 4.28% error. Together, these results establish the commodity home router as practical infrastructure for whole-home activity sensing. The code is open sourced at https://github.com/naisslab/routerweave.

title: WiFo-D: Wireless Foundation Model Based on Discrete Representations
summary: Wireless foundation models have shown strong generalization capabilities across heterogeneous wireless tasks and configurations. However, most existing models rely on continuous representations, limiting ultra-low-overhead channel state information (CSI) feedback, few-shot generalization, and robustness to noise. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a wireless foundation model based on discrete representations (WiFo-D), which learns multi-granularity discrete CSI representations. It comprises a CSI encoder, multi-codebook vector quantization, and a modulation-based decoder, with the learned token maps and quantized features supporting multi-rate CSI feedback, CSI reconstruction, and diverse CSI-related downstream tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong CSI feedback performance at an ultra-low latent compression ratio of 1/32 with 3 bits per token, reducing normalized mean square error (NMSE) by more than 4.7 dB compared with the strongest baseline. Furthermore, for frequency-domain prediction with limited training samples, WiFo-D improves generalization and noise robustness over continuous-representation-based methods. The results also demonstrate its superiority across downstream tasks, including beam prediction, wireless localization, and line-of-sight/non-line-of-sight identification.

title: A generic construction of complex codebooks from functions over Abelian groups
summary: Codebooks with small inner-product correlation play a central role in direct spread code division multiple access communications, space-time coding, compressed sensing, and related areas because they improve system performance. This paper presents a generic construction and a modified construction of complex codebooks from functions on finite Abelian groups. By choosing perfect nonlinear functions, we systematically obtain several families of optimal or asymptotically optimal codebooks with respect to the Welch or Levenshtein bounds. These constructions recover a number of known optimal codebooks and also yield new codebooks with previously unreported parameters.

title: Data-driven Linearization of Operational Dynamics of Soft Open Points in Power Distribution Networks
summary: This paper proposes a novel data-driven linearization of operational power losses in a Soft Open Point (SOP). The proposed learning-based representation, combined with the standard segmentation of the quadratic device capacity inequalities, linearizes the operational dynamics of SOPs in unbalanced power distribution network applications without a significant drop in power loss estimation accuracy. The technique was tested in three applications using a three-phase extension of the IEEE 33-bus network. The case studies include a sizing application for a multi-terminal phase-changing soft open point (PCSOP), an operational optimization application for an active distribution network featuring a PCSOP, and a system simulation engine built for a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) application that trains an agent to optimally dispatch a PCSOP in an unbalanced distribution network. The results of the three case studies were validated against the standard nonlinear AC load-flow representations and point to the efficacy of the proposed solution.

title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
summary: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely.We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.

title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
summary: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.

title: Towards Scale-Up Networking: Challenges and Open Questions
summary: The rapid growth of AI models and the widespread use of distributed training and inference have made inter-accelerator communication a critical system bottleneck. Scale-up fabrics address this bottleneck by combining high per-accelerator bandwidth with low and predictable latency over tightly coupled accelerator domains. However, the appropriate topology, protocol mechanisms, communication semantics, and system integration remain actively debated. We analyze the critical-path communication generated by parallelism strategies and derive the resulting requirements for domain scale, per-accelerator bandwidth, and collective completion latency. We then use these requirements as a framework to examine representative proprietary and open scale-up fabrics, revealing how their physical interconnects, topologies, protocols, and semantics make different trade-offs among performance, scalability, compatibility, and implementation cost. Moreover, based on this analysis and discussions with industry experts, we identify challenges and open problems in physical interconnects and switching, efficient communication, semantics, resource sharing and heterogeneous device interconnection. This paper provides a requirement-driven foundation for analyzing current scale-up fabrics and guiding the design of future systems.

title: 20 ghz longitudinal surface acoustic wave resonators in 100-nm x-cut lithium niobate on silicon carbide
summary: Surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonators above 15~GHz require a fast acoustic mode that retains strong electromechanical coupling ($k^2$). This work reports longitudinal SAW (L-SAW) resonators designed for high $k^2$ in 100-nm X-cut lithium niobate (LN) on 4H silicon carbide (SiC), operating up to 21.7~GHz and reaching a $k^2$ of 8.1\%, a maximum Bode $Q$ of 70, and a figure of merit (FoM) of 5.7 at 20.24~GHz. In this thin-film waveguide, shrinking the wavelength ($λ$) keeps the normalized LN thickness ($h_\mathrm{LN}/λ$) large, sustaining both $k^2$ and acoustic confinement. Conversely, increasing $λ$ from 292 to 471~nm lowers $h_\mathrm{LN}/λ$ from 0.34 to 0.21 and raises the L-SAW phase velocity from 6.32 to 7.05~km/s, within 1.1\% of the 7126-m/s shear-wave velocity of 4H-SiC. As the velocity approaches this limit, more of the acoustic energy spreads into the non-piezoelectric SiC, and $k^2$ falls from its 8.1\% peak at $λ= 322$~nm to 1.7\% at $λ= 471$~nm. No L-SAW resonance is observed for $λ\geq 518$~nm ($h_\mathrm{LN}/λ\leq 0.19$), where the mode becomes leaky. Overall, the FoM stays within 5\% of its maximum for $h_\mathrm{LN}/λ$ between 0.26 to 0.31, defining a design window for L-SAW resonators in thin LN on SiC at K-band and beyond.

title: Self-Supervised Operator Learning for Channel Estimation in Fluid Antenna Systems
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to an IEEE conference
summary: Fluid antenna systems (FAS) have emerged as a promising technology for enhancing wireless communications through adaptive antenna repositioning. Recently, Fourier neural operators (FNOs) have shown strong potential for FAS channel estimation owing to their ability to learn resolution-invariant mappings and generalize across different port densities. However, existing operator learning approaches require densely sampled channel realizations as training labels, whereas a practical receiver only collects noisy pilot observations from a small subset of ports. This mismatch between training requirements and practical channel acquisition poses a major obstacle to deployment. To address this challenge, we develop a self-supervised framework that trains the FNO-based estimator directly from noisy sub-sampled pilots without any labeled channel fields. The proposed objective combines a pilot splitting strategy, which creates supervision at ports hidden from the model input, with a correction based on Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE) that eliminates the measurement noise bias. We prove that this objective admits the same minimum mean square error (MMSE) solution as the ideal supervised criterion. Since the loss relies solely on received pilots, the estimator can be continually adapted online on the live pilot stream. Simulation results show that the self-supervised FNO achieves accuracy comparable to supervised training, generalizes zero-shot to unseen port resolutions, and rapidly recovers from distribution shift via online adaptation.

title: The Prediction-to-Decision Gap: First-Action Informativity in Data-Driven Predictive Control
summary: Model predictive control (MPC) applies only the first input of an optimized sequence before replanning. Do the available data determine this input? We define first-action informativity as agreement across data-compatible models at a fixed history and reference, with common MPC settings. For autoregressive models with exogenous inputs (ARX) and unconstrained quadratic MPC, we show that first-action agreement and prediction agreement under a fixed input sequence do not imply one another. We give structural conditions for action agreement without requiring unique model identification. When actions disagree, we quantify their mean-squared deviation from the fitted model's input under a specific parameter distribution. We approximate this measure using local sensitivities and parameter covariance. Analytical and numerical examples illustrate how model uncertainty affects predictions and actions differently. The framework evaluates model uncertainty through its effect on the first action MPC is about to apply.

title: Mutable State in Enrich-by-Need Security Protocol Analysis
summary:
Security protocol analysis has emphasized message-passing, as this is how different principals interact in authentication, key exchange, and similar functionalities. However, in many protocols a principal also maintains mutable state that limits what actions its local sessions may take; this cross-session state is altered by other local sessions.
  In this paper we show how to represent this cross-session mutable state in the strand space approach to symbolic protocol analysis, and how to implement the resulting ideas in the Cryptographic Protocol Shapes Analyzer CPSA. The key theory is expressed in two axioms characterizing state, plus protocol-specific rules. It leads to tight, specific characterizations of protocol behavior in relevant cases, and aids in developing correct protocols relying on cross-session mutable state.

title: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
summary:
The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way.
  The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.

title: An LLM-Orchestrated Agent Framework for CKM-Assisted Network Deployment Optimization
summary: Channel knowledge maps (CKMs) offer reusable, site-specific radio priors to facilitate environment-aware network planning. However, deploying heterogeneous network nodes to meet diverse performance requirements in complex environments is challenging and requires executable workflows that coordinate scene preparation, candidate-site specification, CKM construction, optimization, and validation. This paper presents a large language model (LLM)-orchestrated agent framework for CKM-assisted network deployment optimization, where an LLM translates high-level requirements into modular, typed, and reproducible planning workflows. In this framework, an LLM layer interprets intent, selects modules, and populates normalized configurations; physics-grounded modules generate scene, CKM, optimization, and validation artifacts; and a deterministic guarded controller performs validation-guided refinement. A common target-candidate-CKM-optimizer interface supports the registration and composition of compatible planning modules, with CKM backends, samplers, and solvers remaining replaceable. We instantiate the proposed framework for base station (BS) deployment, intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) deployment, and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) trajectory planning. An urban-block case study demonstrates automatic scene consistency checks, bounded BS/IRS deployment refinement, and collision- and radio-feasible UAV planning.

title: Optimal Impure $(r,δ)$-Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes with Explicit Minimum Localities
summary:
Quantum locally recoverable codes with $(r,δ)$-locality ($(r,δ)$-qLRCs) are quantum error-correcting codes in which $δ-1$ erased qudits can be recovered by accessing only $r$ other qudits. The minimum locality of a qLRC is the least $r$ such that it has $(r,δ)$-locality. This paper aims to construct optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets and explicit minimum localities, where the optimality is measured by the Singleton-like bound of Guruswami, Kshirsagar, and Trivedi (GKT-optimal). Such qLRCs have particular advantages in recovering as many quantum erasures as possible while operating in parallel and with minimal qudit access overhead.
  We first characterize the recovering sets and the minimum locality of any CSS code by local relative distances, which are relative minimum distances of punctured codes with respect to shortened codes. We then construct impure qLRCs as CSS codes from nested pairs of generalized monomial-Cartesian codes. Grouping the monomials by their degree in the last variable, we reduce both their minimum distances and their local recovery to nested pairs of codes in the remaining variables, and the coordinates with the same values of these variables form disjoint recovering sets. In this way, we obtain four infinite families of GKT-optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets, and determine their minimum localities and the recovering sets attaining them for every admissible $δ$, except for a partial range of $δ$ in one family. These minimum localities need not be monotone in $δ$. In particular, two of the families contain GKT-optimal impure subfamilies of CSS codes CSS$(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})$ with $(r,δ)$-locality for some $r<n-δ+1$ at values of $δ$ for which $\mathcal{C}$ has no classical $(r',δ)$-locality for any $0<r'<n$, where $n$ is the length of $\mathcal{C}$.

title: Data-Driven Hamiltonian Under Parametric Uncertainty
summary: Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the states from which a system can be kept out of an unsafe region, but it requires knowledge of dynamics. The data-driven Hamiltonian (DDH), under a black-box dynamics setting, lower bounds the Hamiltonian directly from trajectory data, which produces a guaranteed conservative safe set. However, it needs a Lipschitz constant of the dynamics, and its bound loosens with the distance from the data. We consider dynamics that are linear in unknown parameters through a known feature vector, with a Gaussian prior on the parameters, and use this structure to construct a parametric DDH. From a few short trajectories with noisy velocity measurements, the parametric DDH lower-bounds the Hamiltonian at all states and costates with a probability of at least $1-δ$. The safe set obtained by replacing the Hamiltonian with this bound is then contained in the true safe set with the same probability. For control-affine systems, evaluating the bound amounts to a second-order cone program, so it can be solved efficiently within existing grid-based and neural PDE solvers. We demonstrate the approach on a two-state system and a six-state lunar lander.

title: User Perceptions of Deceptive In-Vehicle Infotainment User Interfaces
comment: Accepted to the Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium 2027
summary: Modern vehicles collect extensive data about drivers, passengers, and vehicle use, with privacy and consent decisions increasingly mediated through infotainment software. Although dark patterns have been widely studied in web, mobile, and e-commerce interfaces, little is known about how they appear in automotive infotainment systems or how users perceive them. We study this problem through Android Automotive OS (AAOS), conducting a three-phase empirical analysis. First, 26 HCI and privacy annotators audit four OEM AAOS emulators (Honda, Volvo, GM, and Polestar), documenting 17 dark-pattern types across 65 observations. Second, a user study with 100 participants compares OEM-specific implementations of five dark patterns across GMC, Honda, and Volvo, finding that implementation choices affect user perceptions. Third, an independent study with 49 participants compares automotive and e-commerce dark-pattern clips before and after a brief tutorial, showing that automotive's initial rating advantage largely collapses after instruction. Together, the studies identify a sophistication paradox: subtler dark patterns are less likely to trigger user suspicion and may therefore be harder to identify. These findings indicate that oversight should evaluate not just the presence but also the specific implementation of dark patterns.

title: HapBO: Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
summary: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($π: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $α$-$π$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.

title: Lightweight Low-Frequency Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring via Karhunen-Loève Feature Distillation and Temporal Convolutional Networks
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid. S. Peeris, P. Thennakoon and P. Sumanasekara contributed equally
summary: Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) is a critical enabler for demand-side management which allows for smart grid optimization. A deployment-ready NILM solution necessitates three key features: accurate disaggregation, low-frequency sampling, and low computational cost. This paper proposes a lightweight, edge-oriented NILM framework that combines activity-boundary-aware synthetic data augmentation with Karhunen-Loève Transform (KLT) feature extraction and a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). The augmentation stage extracts and recombines complete or near-complete appliance activation segments so that the model can be trained without new fully labeled household aggregates. The KLT filter bank extracts decorrelated, appliance-informed temporal features which are then fed into a compact TCN along with the original aggregate for energy disaggregation. Evaluations on two standard NILM datasets, UK-DALE and REDD, at 10-s sampling and with leave-one-house-out testing, demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves comparable or superior disaggregation accuracy relative to NILMFormer, BERT4NILM, BiLSTM, and BiGRU. The computational footprint of the framework is 31,009 parameters, the fewest of the five models compared, and on a single CPU thread it needs 2.78 ms per 1000 samples, 84-95% less than the baselines. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for low-frequency smart-meter NILM.

title: Self-Orthogonal MDS Principal-Ideal Codes
summary: We investigate Euclidean self-orthogonality and the generalized Reed--Solomon (GRS) property for coefficient-vector codes generated by a monic polynomial $g$ and its shifts $xg,\ldots,x^{k-1}g$, of length $n=r+k$ and dimension $k$, where $°g=r$ and $3\le k\le r$. We give a complete classification, over any algebraically closed field, of the generators for which these codes are both self-orthogonal and GRS. Such generators have either distinct roots in a geometric progression satisfying explicit order and scalar conditions, or a single repeated root in certain positive characteristics. In particular, only finitely many generators occur for fixed $r$, $k$, and characteristic. We determine their maximal self-orthogonal lengths, show that the corresponding maximal-length codes are cyclic or negacyclic, and obtain exact generator counts over finite fields, together with the least fields of definition. In contrast, when $3\le k<r$, we prove that every algebraically closed field supports infinitely many pairwise monomially inequivalent self-orthogonal non-GRS maximum distance separable (MDS) codes in this family. Consequently, arbitrarily many such codes can be realized over a common finite extension of any prescribed finite field, while remaining inequivalent and non-GRS over its algebraic closure.

title: Cone-Constrained Safe Policy Learning With Finite-Step Improvement Guarantees
summary: One central challenge in safe reinforcement learning is improving task performance while reducing infeasibility risk, especially when long-term constraint consequences are difficult to represent and optimize. We propose the Constraint Aggregation Function (CAF), a learnable feasibility-oriented representation of long-horizon risk that satisfies a discounted Bellman recursion and admits a unique fixed point. The proposed CAF induces a risk advantage that measures the reduction in predicted unsafety relative to the current policy. Building on this representation, we develop Cone-Constrained Policy Optimization (CCPO), which uses the CAF-induced risk advantage to define a risk descent direction. The proposed CCPO resolves conflicts between task ascent and risk descent through gradient projection, selecting the final update from the relative interior of a constructed safety cone. Under standard smoothness assumptions and a step-size bound, this update guarantees simultaneous task improvement and risk reduction. Numerically, CCPO stays feasible with a 1.05% mean optimality gap in emergency braking and attains low constraint violations on safety-critical benchmarks.

title: Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models
summary: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.

title: Long-Range Video Presentation Attack Detection: A Three-Class Benchmark Across 1-100 m and Two Sensor Types
summary: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) systems deployed in border control and airport surveillance are constrained by a critical assumption: subjects are captured at close range, typically under one meter. No existing benchmark systematically addresses multi-distance capture, diverse environmental conditions, and concurrent spoofing and occlusion-based attacks, leaving deployed models underprepared for real-world scenarios. We introduce a video-based PAD dataset of 374,000+ frames from 261 unique identities collected across five standoff distances (1 m-100 m) under indoor and outdoor conditions using a DSLR camera (C) and a mobile sensor (M), with three-class labels: live, spoof, and props (occlusions); models are trained and evaluated on video clips rather than single frames. We fine-tune and benchmark four CNN architectures: MobileNetV3, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ResNet-50. The higher-resolution DSLR maintains near-perfect spoof classification rate across all distances, while the lower-resolution mobile sensor degrades sharply beyond 50 m, with props classification rate dropping to 55% at 75 m for MobileNetV3. EfficientNet achieves the best overall performance (98.48% accuracy, ACER 2.01%). Generalization tests on unseen attack datasets yield 89-94% accuracy, validating cross-domain robustness. These results establish capture distance and sensor resolution as critical but underexplored axes of PAD difficulty. The dataset will be publicly released under an End-User License Agreement to support reproducible long-range PAD research.

title: A closed-loop agentic research environment for MRI development within Siemens IDEA platform
summary: Motivation: Testing new ideas in MRI can require substantial effort to learn sequence programming and reconstruction tools and to debug implementations before the scientific question can be addressed. Goals: Reduce the implementation and debugging burden of testing MRI ideas while retaining researcher control of scientific decisions. Approach: We developed an environment where LLM agents develop sequences in the native Siemens IDEA platform, evaluate them through Bloch simulation and reconstruction, and further iteratively refine them using scanner feedback. Results: As test cases, the agentic environment was used to implement and validate a GIRF-based gradient-calibration sequence and reconstruction in approximately 4 hours, and to develop and optimize a rapid 3-second multichannel calibration scan in approximately 12 hours of researcher-guided iteration.

title: Feedback-Free FDD Cell-Free Massive MIMO With Sparse AP Activation and Dual-Mode Precoding
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology
summary: This correspondence enables practical frequency-division duplex (FDD) operation in cell-free massive MIMO via two mechanisms. Sparse access-point (AP) activation reduces downlink pilot overhead to enable coherent detection, while angle-reciprocity precoding steers beams using only uplink-estimated angles, eliminating channel feedback entirely. A load-adaptive dual-mode optimizer further enhances performance: closed-form signal-to-leakage-and-noise-ratio precoding for high-load rate boosting, or semidefinite relaxation for low-load power minimization. Simulations verify its superiority over existing feedback-free FDD solutions in spectral and energy efficiency, and its robustness to angle errors, reciprocity mismatch, and multipath.

title: DeoPC: Data-Enabled Output-Feedback Predictive Control for State Regulation
summary: Constrained regulation of the internal state of an unknown linear system is challenging when only input-output measurements are available online. In this work, we develop a data-enabled output-feedback predictive control (DeoPC) framework for constrained state regulation using input-output data. Specifically, a data-driven state estimate is constructed from past input-output data via a subspace-based singular value decomposition. Based on this state representation, we formulate a predictive controller that directly penalizes the state and control effort while enforcing the system constraints. Under persistent excitation and initialization conditions, we establish recursive feasibility and closed-loop stability of DeoPC in both noise-free and bounded-noise settings. In addition, we show that DeoPC can be calibrated to the physical state coordinates using a few offline state measurements, or treated as a model predictive control tuning problem when no state measurements are available. The effectiveness of DeoPC is demonstrated through simulations on an unstable batch reactor system.

title: Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization for Bitcoin Custody
summary: A compromised cryptocurrency withdrawal backend can request signatures on unauthorized payments. Previously signed transactions may remain spendable after pause or become spendable again after a reorganization. Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization (RBWA) orders permits against pause in a replicated journal and restores exposure when its closing evidence disappears from Bitcoin's active chain. An optional route delays large payouts and permits independent cold recovery. Direct payments confirm in one block on regtest, and staged payments confirm in three or seven at delays of two or six. After rollback, a replayed recovery can win or lose to an already exported mature payout. Authenticated receipts can revoke one signing lease in a shared wallet. In matched synthetic schedules, probes reduce permits through compromised leases from 20 to 9 out of 33, with one false fence. Two held-out HTTP workloads find equal fixed-threshold precision for boosted audit and probe-augmented detectors. The audit fields already expose the probe authentication outcome. Live tests verify an exact maintenance exception and add a file marker as a distinct source. The marker fences a compromised lease that RPC-only audit misses. Audit with the same file-read evidence also fences a reader who bypasses the probe. The results tie the benefit of active probing to which evidence the operator can obtain.

title: Fast and Memory-Light Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with the DISCO Index in R
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. R package discoCVI available on CRAN
summary: DISCO is a recent internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that, unlike earlier indices, also evaluates the quality of noise labels. The discoCVI package makes DISCO available in R. This article describes the design of the package and a typical workflow, in which DISCO is used to compare clusterings and to choose the parameters of HDBSCAN without ground truth, followed by the implementation introduced in version 0.2.0. DISCO is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. We show that every quantity DISCO needs can be read off the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, so that the index can be computed exactly with memory that grows linearly with the number of points, while the running time remains quadratic as in the original definition. The implementation is tested against the previous version, agrees with the original Python implementation to within $3 \times 10^{-13}$, and corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. In benchmarks, discoCVI is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous version for 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for 500 to 8,000 points, using a fraction of the memory of both, and it scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory.

title: Signed Powers-of-Two Greedy Vector Approximation of Zadoff-Chu Sequences
summary: This paper explores the use of sums of signed powers-of-two (SOPOT) for a representation suitable for multiplierless applications of ZC sequences, where multiplications are reduced to a prescribed number of shift-and-add operations. The SOPOT representation is achieved using a greedy algorithm that outperforms other approaches for multiplierless approximations, such as CORDIC and CSD. The proposed algorithm is based on the matching pursuits using generalized bit planes (MPGBP), and the proposed modification enables robustness to hyperparameter tuning. The resulting sequences retain, to some extent, the good autocorrelation properties of ZC, as shown in a matched-filter detection simulation. This corroborates to their use in various practical applications across mainstream cellular systems and devices requiring moderate computational cost.

title: Asymptotic Bounds for Codes in Toroidal Distance
summary: The toroidal distance naturally describes the geometry of codes over \(\mathbb Z_q\), where distances are measured modulo \(q\). In this paper, we study asymptotic bounds for codes in \(\mathbb Z_q^n\) under the toroidal metric. We first derive an explicit asymptotic lower bound from the classical Gilbert--Varshamov bounds for the Hamming and Lee metrics, which serves as a baseline for comparison. We then develop a saddle-point approach for the toroidal metric, which yields an asymptotic Gilbert--Varshamov lower bound and an asymptotic Hamming-type upper bound. For \(3\mid q\), we embed ternary Hamming codes into \(\mathbb Z_q^n\) and obtain another asymptotic lower bound for the toroidal metric. In addition, we derive an asymptotic lower bound for Maximum Toroidal Distance (MTD) codes. We compare these lower bounds with the baseline and prove that they are nontrivial in the corresponding parameter ranges. Finally, we compare the asymptotic bounds numerically.

title: A four-level executable validation protocol for evaluating LLM-generated topology specifications of physics-based HVAC digital twins
